title: Priority-Driven Kernel Scheduler: Design and Runbook
author: Emily Chen
summary: Specification and operational runbook for the Priority-Driven Kernel Scheduler used by Redwood's serving runtime. Covers design rationale, scheduling algorithm, configuration knobs, SLO mappings, metric instrumentation, rollout steps, and incident mitigation playbooks for latency and throughput regressions.
body:
Purpose and scope

This document defines the Priority-Driven Kernel Scheduler (PDKS) used in the Redwood serving runtime. It describes the design goals, algorithm, configuration surface, expected SLO behavior, and operational runbook for on-call engineers and release owners. The PDKS module is responsible for deciding kernel assignment, preemption, and batching windows for GPU workers (processes: rw-runtime-worker, rw-batching-proxy), and for enforcing tenant and model-level latency/throughput policies.

Why a priority-driven scheduler?

- Production goals: meet 95th/99th percentile latency SLOs for interactive (chat/generation) workloads while maintaining cost-efficient GPU utilization for background/throughput jobs (embeddings, bulk rerank).
- Mixed workload environment: hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private clusters all run on the same runtime binary; scheduling logic must support strict isolation for Dedicated pools and best-effort background work for shared pools.
- Operational predictability: explicit priority tiers make rollback and mitigation simpler (e.g., throttle low-priority batching windows rather than kill running kernels).

Design overview

1) Priority tiers
- P0 (latency-critical): interactive chat/generation requests with SLA/enterprise flags. High preemption weight, small batching windows (configurable min_batch = 1), KV cache locality pinned.
- P1 (standard): normal API requests. Balanced batching and latency.
- P2 (background): embeddings, bulk transforms, scheduled jobs. Large batching windows, throttled when P0/P1 backlog grows.
- P3 (best-effort): offline jobs, non-critical re-runs. Lowest priority, allowed to be paused or migrated.

2) Key scheduling primitives
- Kernel assignment: map model_variant -> kernel_profile. The kernel selection subsystem consults a per-model kernel_profile table (see config table below) that includes preferred CUDA/cuBLAS/cuDNN kernels and quantized-code paths.
- Preemption policy: preemptible=true on P1/P2/P3; P0 requests set preemptible=false. Preemption is implemented via checkpointing KV cache and fast context switch (10–30ms target).
- Fairshare buckets: soft quotas per-customer and per-tenant to avoid noisy neighbor across P1/P2. Buckets are refilled every 60s.
- Batching window adjustment: dynamic window adjusts between min_batch and max_batch based on measured inter-arrival time and current SLO pressure.

3) Observability surface
- Metrics emitted (Prometheus names):
  - rw_scheduler_queue_length{priority}
  - rw_scheduler_avg_batch_size{model,priority}
  - rw_scheduler_preemptions_total{cause}
  - rw_kernel_kernel_selection_latency_ms
  - rw_scheduler_kernel_switch_latency_ms (target < 30 ms)
  - rw_scheduler_gpu_occupancy_percent
  - rw_scheduler_slo_violation_count{model,priority,percentile}

4) SLO mapping and expected behavior
- Interactive (P0): 99th percentile latency target <= 300 ms (local processing, small context lengths). When P0 backlog > 10% of worker queue, scheduler will: (a) reduce batching window to min_batch for affected workers, (b) throttle P2/P3 intake by 50%, (c) signal autoscaler with priority reason = "P0_backlog".
- Standard (P1): 95th percentile latency <= 750 ms. If P1 SLO breaks, scheduler raises preemption aggressiveness for P2 and reduces P1 batching windows by up to 30%.
- Background (P2): Throughput-oriented; no hard latency SLO, but throttled under pressure.

Configuration reference (key knobs)

| knob_name | default | description | safe_range | owner_service |
|-----------|---------|-------------|------------|---------------|
| min_batch_size | 1 | Minimum number of requests to form a kernel batch for a worker | 1–8 | rw-batching-proxy |
| max_batch_size | 64 | Maximum allowed batch size per kernel invocation | 16–1024 | rw-batching-proxy |
| preemption_grace_ms | 30 | Time allowed to checkpoint KV cache and context-switch | 10–200 | rw-runtime-worker |
| fairshare_window_s | 60 | Seconds for fairshare refill | 30–600 | rw-scheduler-service |
| p0_backlog_threshold_pct | 10 | Percent of queue backlog to trigger P0 emergency actions | 5–25 | rw-scheduler-service |
| dynamic_batch_alpha | 0.6 | Weight for exponential smoothing on batch size calc | 0.1–0.95 | rw-batching-proxy |

Kernel selection table (example snippet)

- Model family: llama2-70b
  - preferred_kernel: fused_attention_v3
  - quantized_profile: q4_0 (fast_path=true)
  - recommended_max_seq: 4096
- Model family: mosaic-1b
  - preferred_kernel: attention_split_kv
  - quantized_profile: q5_1 (fast_path=false)
  - recommended_max_seq: 2048

Operational runbook: alerts and first actions

Triggering alerts (examples):
1) ALERT: rw_scheduler_slo_violation_count{priority="P0",percentile="99"} > 0 for 3m
2) ALERT: rw_scheduler_gpu_occupancy_percent < 25% for 10m (possible kernel contention or driver issue)
3) ALERT: rw_scheduler_preemptions_total increased by > 5x in 5m window

First-response checklist (page owner: runtime-oncall)
1) Acknowledge pager; post to #runtime-ops with alert details and diagnostics link.
2) Run quick health queries (Grafana):
   - Check rw_scheduler_queue_length by priority and model
   - Check rw_scheduler_avg_batch_size and GPU occupancy per node
3) If P0 SLO violated:
   - Execute emergency throttle: curl -X POST https://ops-api.internal/v1/scheduler/adjust -d '{"action":"throttle","priorities":["P2","P3"],"factor":0.5}'
   - Scale up Dedicated capacity: run infra script: ./tools/scale_pool --pool=dedicated-default --delta=+2 --reason="P0_slo_emergency"
   - If preemptions spiking, check kernel_switch_latency_ms: if > 150ms, escalate to infra and GPU-firmware teams.
4) If GPU occupancy low across nodes: check driver logs (/var/log/nvidia-installer.log) and dmesg for ECC/PCIe errors; consider node drain and GC.

Mitigation flows (detailed)

- Flow A: Temporary P2 suspension
  1. Verify backlog levels and confirm P0 impact.
  2. Use operator API to set intake_allowed=false for tags matching background_jobs for 15m.
  3. Monitor P0 latency; when 99p returns to target for 5 minutes, re-enable intake at 50% and ramp.

- Flow B: Kernel-path fallback
  1. If kernel_selection_latency_ms spikes and model fails to launch optimized kernel, fallback to generic_kernel for affected model_variant via: curl -X POST https://ops-api.internal/v1/kernel/fallback -d '{"model":"<model_variant>","to":"generic_kernel"}'
  2. Notify model-onboarding and performance teams to triage kernel build.

Rollout checklist for changes to scheduler (release owner required)
1) Design review completed and reviewers signed off.
2) Unit and integration tests in CI: scheduler unit tests, simulated traffic harness with P0/P1/P2 mixes.
3) Canary deploy to a single Dedicated pool (tag: canary-scheduler-1) with traffic split 1% for 24 hours.
4) Run perf harness: ./tools/perf-harness --profile=interactive-heavy --duration=30m and validate rw_scheduler_* metrics.
5) Gradual ramp: 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% across non-critical pools over 48–72h with rollback gates after each step.

Troubleshooting examples (commands)
- Inspect per-worker queue: curl -s http://localhost:6060/debug/queues | jq '.'
- Force a kernel-selection dry run: curl -X POST http://localhost:6060/debug/kernel_dryrun -d '{"model":"llama2-70b","sequence_length":1024}'
- Dump KV cache stats: docker exec -it rw-worker /bin/sh -c 'rw-kvtool stats --format=json'

Testing and benchmarking guidance

- Use the benchmarking suite job-profile: interactive-p0-random (available in perf repo). Key expectations: 99p latency for small context (<= 512 tokens) should be within 300ms with P0 traffic at 20 rps per worker.
- Synthetic stress tests: mix P0 at 10rps, P1 at 50rps and P2 batch jobs to saturate GPU memory. Verify preemption triggers and kernel_switch_latency_ms under 30ms.

Known limitations and future work

- Checkpoint cost: KV cache checkpointing can exceed preemption_grace_ms for very large contexts (>= 32K). Future: incremental checkpointing and CRDT-style partial restore.
- Multi-GPU scheduling: current algorithm optimizes per-GPU workers independently and has suboptimal cross-GPU placement for large model sharding. Future: global placement optimizer with communication-cost model.
- Heterogeneous hardware: CPU fallback paths for quantized kernels are immature; expect 2x latency when falling back to CPU.

Appendices

A. Glossary
- KV cache: key-value attention cache used to accelerate autoregressive decoding.
- Kernel profile: pre-built binary path and launch config for a model variant.
- Preemption grace: configured time budget to serialize and checkpoint in-flight state.
